strengths: Well-motivated empirical study: Figure 1 clearly demonstrates a fundamental and previously undocumented trade-off between long-term planning and short-term precision in action chunking, which has independent scientific value

Elegant and practical solution: MoH is conceptually simple (multi-horizon processing with lightweight linear gating requiring only 2k parameters) and achieves minimal computational overhead (~2% in Figure 6), making it truly plug-and-play

Comprehensive experimental validation: Extensive tests across multiple benchmarks (LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0), multiple base models (π₀, π₀.₅, πᵣₑ𝓰), policy types (flow-matching, regression), and both simulated and real-world settings with consistent improvements

Thorough ablation studies: Tables 2-3 and Figures 5-6 systematically validate each component (horizon density, loss reweighting, gating balance, computational overhead), with clear mechanistic insights
Strong empirical results: Achieves 99% success rate on LIBERO mixed-task setting and consistent improvements across all settings, establishing new state-of-the-art

Creative dynamic inference variant: Algorithm 1's cross-horizon consensus scheme achieves 2.5× throughput improvement while maintaining performance, demonstrating practical value beyond the base method
Honest and thorough evaluation: Appendix D provides detailed failure case analysis distinguishing between environment artifacts and model limitations, supporting reproducibility claims
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: The solution combines well-established techniques (multi-scale processing, softmax gating, balance loss from mixture-of-experts). While practically useful, it represents incremental engineering rather than methodological advance

Insufficient mechanistic understanding: The paper documents the horizon trade-off empirically but does not explain its root cause. Why does increased horizon harm early-step predictions? What do different horizons learn? Visualization and analysis of learned representations would strengthen claims

Under-justified design choices: (1) Balance loss weight λ_bal=10⁻³ appears arbitrary without ablation; (2) Horizon configuration H={3,6,...,30} only thoroughly tested without exploring the space; (3) Dynamic inference parameters (n,m,r) require manual tuning with no principled selection method; (4) L₁ disagreement metric may be suboptimal for certain action types

Limited real-world evaluation: Only 3 tasks with 10 rollouts each (small sample size), all short-to-medium horizon, trained with only 30 demonstrations. No data efficiency curves, cross-embodiment analysis, or evidence of scaling to complex real-world scenarios

Incomplete experimental analysis: (1) No comparison with alternative multi-scale approaches or curriculum learning baselines; (2) No analysis of which task phases/objects benefit from which horizons; (3) LIBERO evaluation executes only first 5 actions, potentially masking long-term planning issues; (4) No statistical significance testing despite small improvement margins in some cases

Dynamic inference validation gaps: Only tested on LIBERO-Long subset; Figure 8 shows parameter r is task-sensitive but no guidance provided; limited analysis of when benefits materialize; feels disconnected from main MoH contribution

Reproducibility and generalization concerns: (1) Behavior undefined for using fewer training horizons at test time; (2) Hyperparameter sensitivity not explored; (3) Generalization to other VLM backbones not tested; (4) Cross-dataset evaluation absent

Presentation and notation issues: Attention mask mechanism not detailed in Method section; training objective (Eq. 17) interaction between three loss terms lacks clear explanation; some mathematical notation inconsistencies (dimensions of A_t^(h))

strengths: Clear identification and empirical demonstration of the horizon trade-off in action chunking (Figure 1) with good motivation
Elegant and practical plug-and-play solution with minimal overhead (2k parameters, <10% training cost increase) applicable across VLA architectures
Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning two simulation benchmarks, real-world tasks, and multiple base models with well-designed ablation studies validating each component
Solid empirical results with consistent gains across settings; π₀.₅ achieves 99% on LIBERO mixed-task setting with only 30k iterations
Thorough ablations (Table 2-3) clearly showing that improvements come from multi-horizon collaboration rather than loss reweighting alone, and demonstrating the necessity of the balance loss
Honest discussion of limitations with detailed failure mode analysis (Appendix D) acknowledging environmental artifacts and VLA perception limitations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core approach is straightforward application of mixture-of-experts (acknowledged but not differentiated); gating mechanism is standard linear softmax and balance loss borrowed from MoE literature

Modest empirical improvements on near-saturated benchmarks (typically 1-2% on LIBERO, which already achieves 97-99%); overstated 'state-of-the-art' claims given competing methods already reach similar performance

Lack of theoretical understanding of the horizon trade-off mechanism: why does it exist (optimization difficulty vs. capacity vs. regularization?) and why does this fusion strategy resolve it? No principled analysis provided

Insufficient guidance for hyperparameter selection: horizon set H={3,6,...,30} appears arbitrary; no principled method for new domains; dynamic inference introduces heuristic hyperparameters (r, n, m) without thorough sensitivity analysis

Dynamic inference scheme (Algorithm 1) underdeveloped: threshold computation is heuristic, limited failure mode analysis, and feels orthogonal to main contribution rather than well-integrated; hyperparameter choices lack justification

Small-scale real-world validation: only 3 tasks with 10 rollouts each (30 total trials), no statistical significance testing, insufficient to support broad real-world claims; one interesting failure (π₀.₅ vs π₀) not investigated

Missing mechanistic analyses: no investigation of whether horizons specialize in different task types, no visualization of learned gating patterns beyond Figure 5, gradient flow through padded positions not discussed

Narrow scope limited to action chunking in VLAs on manipulation; generalization to other embodied AI tasks (navigation, assembly) unclear; applicability primarily to full-attention transformers (already standard)

strengths: Clear problem motivation with systematic empirical demonstration of the horizon trade-off (Figure 1)
Simple yet effective solution with minimal computational overhead (2k parameters), making it broadly applicable to full-attention action modules
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple benchmarks (LIBERO, RoboTwin2.0), model variants (π0, π0.5, πreg), and real-world robot experiments
Thorough ablation studies validating each component: horizon density, loss reweighting, gating necessity, and balance loss impact
Innovative dynamic inference mechanism via cross-horizon consensus achieving 2.5× throughput improvement while maintaining performance
Excellent presentation with clear visualizations, comprehensive supplementary materials, and honest failure case analysis
Consistent improvements across diverse settings, achieving new state-of-the-art on LIBERO (99% average success)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the gating mechanism is a straightforward Softmax-normalized weighted sum, essentially a simplified mixture-of-experts applied to horizons

Shallow mechanistic understanding: the paper demonstrates that MoH works but provides limited insight into why different horizons capture complementary information or which task properties favor specific horizon lengths
Horizon selection lacks principled guidance: default H = {3, 6, ..., 30} with stride d=3 appears empirically determined; no principled method for selecting horizons in new domains
Balance loss formulation (Eqs. 14-16) with horizon-dependent interval partitioning appears ad-hoc and lacks theoretical justification
Real-world validation is limited in scope: only 3 tasks with 10 trials each; tasks are relatively simple; platform details partially redacted

Incomplete baseline comparisons: primarily compares against single-horizon baselines; missing comparisons to curriculum learning, hierarchical action planning, or other multi-scale temporal approaches
Dynamic inference hyperparameter sensitivity not fully explored: Algorithm 1 introduces parameters (n, m, r) requiring tuning with limited guidance for practitioners
Modest improvements on individual task suites (1-2% typical), though consistent; LIBERO 99% represents ensemble effects rather than proportional gains per suite
Lack of statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; some improvements are within potential noise margins
Generalization questions unaddressed: all experiments use PaliGemma backbone; no exploration of transfer to other VLMs or cross-task gating weight reuse

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification with clear empirical evidence of the horizon trade-off (Figure 1); different task complexities demonstrably prefer different horizons

Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple models (π0, π0.5, StarVLA, πreg), three diverse benchmarks (LIBERO, RoboTwin, RoboCasa), and real-world robotic tasks with consistent improvements

Strong ablation studies (Tables 3-4) effectively isolating each component; particularly compelling is showing identical-horizon branches provide minimal gains, confirming horizon diversity is essential
Practical design with only 2k additional parameters and negligible inference latency overhead (~5%), making the method truly plug-and-play for existing VLA models
Honest discussion of limitations and failure cases in Appendices I-J, demonstrating scientific rigor and transparency about remaining challenges
Achieves new state-of-the-art on LIBERO (99% average success with π0.5) and demonstrates practical dynamic inference benefit (2.5× throughput)
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: mixture-of-scales with gating is well-established; the application to action chunking is straightforward and incremental rather than introducing fundamental new insights

Shallow mechanistic understanding of the horizon trade-off; paper identifies the phenomenon empirically but doesn't explain why longer horizons degrade short-term precision or whether this is fundamental to transformers or specific to action chunking

Horizon selection lacks principled guidance; the choice of {3, 6, ..., 30} appears ad-hoc with no systematic procedure for practitioners to select appropriate horizons for new domains, and sensitivity analysis in Table 8 is limited

Dynamic inference mechanism (Algorithm 1) appears ad-hoc with multiple hyperparameters (r, n, m) lacking thorough sensitivity analysis; threshold design using mean of first n steps is heuristic and choice of L1 disagreement is unexplained

Modest empirical gains especially concerning at performance saturation: no improvement on LIBERO-Spatial (98.8% both), 3.4% on RoboCasa with high variance, often 1-3% elsewhere; no error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance testing provided

Training time overhead non-trivial (26% increase for π0.5 with stride 3 per Appendix B) but understated as 'negligible'; memory overhead during training not discussed; trade-off between cost and 1-3% gains not clearly quantified

Real-world experiments underpowered with only 4 tasks on single platform, limited rollouts (10-20 per task), unexplained anomalies (π0.5 worse than π0 on T2), and insufficient evidence of generalization
Key design choices lack ablation or justification: λbal=10^-3, λind=1 set 'empirically' without analysis; πreg is custom implementation not released by original authors, affecting reproducibility
Critical technical details missing: exact padding procedure for A^(h)_t, mask values, computational complexity analysis, guidance on pre-training deployment (Appendix C only)
Insights don't generalize beyond action chunking in VLAs; no discussion of applicability to other sequential prediction tasks or broader temporal multi-scale modeling

strengths: Identifies and systematically demonstrates a real, previously unstudied trade-off in action chunking horizons (Figure 1), motivating the work clearly
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across LIBERO, RoboTwin, RoboCasa with multiple base models (π0, π0.5, StarVLA, πreg) and real-world validation, showing consistent improvements
Practical plug-and-play approach with minimal overhead (~10% training, 2k parameters), genuinely useful for practitioners
Thorough ablation studies (Section 4.3, Appendix F) effectively isolate contributions and validate all major components
Well-documented with extensive appendices covering hyperparameters, latency analysis, failure modes, and qualitative demonstrations
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: straightforward application of well-established mixture-of-experts and gating mechanisms to ensemble multiple horizons, lacking methodological innovation

Insufficient theoretical understanding: identifies the trade-off empirically but provides no mechanistic insight into why it exists; per-step error analysis (Table 9) is too shallow; cross-horizon consensus mechanism lacks principled justification

Modest empirical improvements without statistical rigor: most gains are 0.2-1.3% on LIBERO, 3.4% on RoboCasa; no confidence intervals or significance tests despite stochastic evaluation and small margins; short training (30k iterations) raises saturation questions

Contradictory design: balance loss Lbal actively prevents learning strong horizon preferences (Table 10 shows ~0.3% differences), yet paper claims task-adaptive learning; unclear why preventing specialization is beneficial given the motivation

Weak real-world validation: only 4 simple tasks with 30 demonstrations; limited rollouts per task (10 in most cases); no comparison with other SOTA methods on real robots; insufficient investigation of mentioned failure modes

Unfair baseline comparisons: Table 1 mixes methods with different batch sizes (32 vs. 128-192), datasets, and iteration counts; ATE comparison (Table 5) is unfair since ATE targets different problem (temporal smoothing, not horizon fusion)

Limited hyperparameter analysis: horizon configuration {3,6,...,30} not thoroughly studied; balance loss weight (λ_bal=10^-3) lacks sensitivity analysis; dynamic inference has three hyperparameters (r,n,m) with minimal guidance; no ablation on horizon range bounds

Presentation issues: Method section is dense with abrupt transitions between components; design choices (linear gating, specific balance loss formulation) lack justification; confuses 'mixture' with 'ensemble' despite Lbal preventing true specialization

Reproducibility concerns: code availability not mentioned; πreg design is ad-hoc (Appendix D) since π0 doesn't release regression version; horizon-specific attention mask implementation details absent

Narrow scope of generalization: no evaluation on tasks longer than training trajectories; no extreme horizon ranges tested; limited OOD generalization analysis; Appendix I notes environment artifacts/simulator bugs inflating reported success rates

strengths: Clearly identifies and empirically validates an important trade-off in VLA action horizons that hasn't been systematically studied, with convincing evidence across LIBERO task suites
Proposes an elegant, simple solution (action rearrangement + lightweight gating) that is truly plug-and-play for any full-attention action module with minimal computational overhead

Provides comprehensive experimental validation across multiple VLA architectures (π0, π0.5, StarVLA, πreg), benchmarks (LIBERO, RoboTwin, RoboCasa), and real-world tasks with consistent improvements and new SOTA on LIBERO (99%)

Includes exceptionally thorough ablation studies that convincingly isolate each component's contribution (horizon density, diversity, balance loss) and demonstrate improvements stem from diverse horizons rather than generic ensemble effects
Introduces a practical dynamic inference scheme via cross-horizon consensus that achieves 2.5× throughput while maintaining superior performance, adding genuine novelty
Demonstrates strong rigor with identical random seeds across comparisons, multiple seeds for real-world experiments, detailed hyperparameter specifications, and comprehensive failure analysis
Provides empirical evidence for the trade-off mechanism through per-step action error analysis (Table 9), showing per-step L1 error increases monotonically with horizon on short-horizon tasks
Excellent presentation with clear writing, well-designed figures, and comprehensive appendix including task-adaptive weight analysis and threshold justification
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method combines multi-horizon prediction, softmax gating, and mixture-of-experts balance loss—all existing techniques. While effective, individual components are straightforward with no algorithmic innovation

Core mechanism not fully understood: unclear why this approach is better than training on mixed-horizon data or whether improvements come from temporal horizon diversity specifically versus generic ensemble effects. Table 4 shows identical horizons give only 97.9% (vs 99.0% for diverse), but analysis of what different horizons learn is missing

LIBERO benchmark is saturated: π0.5 baseline at 97.7% vs MoH at 99.0% equals only 1.3% absolute improvement; many individual tasks at/near ceiling (Object 100%, Goal 98.8%). Appendix I reveals many remaining failures are environmental bugs rather than policy limitations, making true improvement magnitude unclear

Real-world validation is limited: only 4 tasks with 10-20 rollouts each (small statistical samples), relatively simple tasks (pick-place, pouring), and results in Figure 7(b) show modest improvements without confidence intervals or error bars

Dynamic inference introduces design choices that lack principled justification: Algorithm 1 hyperparameters (n, m, r) require tuning; threshold design (mean of first n steps) is empirically motivated with limited ablation (only r varied in Figure 6); unclear sensitivity to these choices on diverse tasks

Horizon selection strategy is not principled: H={3,6,...,30} chosen empirically for LIBERO; Hmax=30 shown optimal for this benchmark but task-dependence unclear; practitioners lack guidance for selecting horizons on new domains despite showing robustness to configurations

Training overhead not fully addressed: Figure 8 shows 28% increase in training time (0.68→0.87 s/iter) for dense horizons; while claimed 'minimal,' this is non-trivial for billion-parameter pretraining. Sparse-horizon pretraining (1.4% overhead) mentioned in Appendix C but not validated

Subtle task-adaptive weight patterns: Table 10 shows only minor weight shifts across tasks (h=3 goes from 9.09% to 8.93% across Spatial→Long); unclear whether these subtle differences drive performance gains or if the benefit comes simply from having diverse options to average over
